plan.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo) is a pill, so why can it still cause nausea? GI side effects on the label vs placebo
plan.angle: Sentence 1 as planned. By 6 s: 'The US label lists nausea as a common side effect: X% on orforglipron vs Y% on placebo.' (Use L1's verified numbers, arms and population.) Then a plain sentence from label 12.1: 'Like the injected GLP-1 medicines, orforglipron is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. It works on the same receptor, just in pill form.' Drop 'how you take it doesn't change what it does' and any explanation of what causes the nausea. Timing goes in label wording as a trial pattern. Keep the 2 untagged tips, the severe-stomach-pain emergency card, the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.
plan.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo): Why Can a Pill Cause Nausea? #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1: it rides the fresh Canadian and Australian approvals (the radar suggested this exact question), stays a felt-symptom Short, and drives viewers to the Foundayo long video. | fact-check: The topic is fine, but one planned sentence overstates the science. 'How you take it doesn't change what it does' isn't label wording and isn't strictly true. Orforglipron is a non-peptide small molecule, and its absorption and dosing differ from the injectable peptides. Section 12.1 supports only that it is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Nothing in the label says nausea comes from receptor action and not from the route, so don't imply that cause either. The nausea rate per arm vs placebo must match L1's verified script exactly, including the drug, the arms, the ATTAIN-1 population and 72 weeks. Timing goes in the label's words ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time', if that is the Foundayo wording) and is framed as a trial pattern. The severe-stomach-pain line follows the label's pancreatitis wording and keeps 'right away'. The related-video target should be the Side Effects video until L1 is live.

Orforglipron (Foundayo) is a once-daily pill, but stomach side effects were still the most common in its 72-week trial, mostly mild to moderate.
Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Get medical help right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Orforglipron
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: The script is accurate and safe. src1 (Wharton S et al., NEJM, ATTAIN-1, PMID 40960239, published 16 Sep 2025) exists. A search of the abstract and two secondary summaries (ACC journal scan, Healio) confirmed that it describes orforglipron as an oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist. They also confirmed the 72-week treatment period, adults with obesity without diabetes, and that the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal and mostly mild to moderate. The script's wording keeps that hedge. The ATTAIN-1 population on the card matches the channel's standard scope. S2-3 makes no claim about what causes the nausea. The tips in S2-4 are hedged with "may help" and correctly carry no source tag. The closing follows the template: the prescriber line as one card, then the severe-stomach-pain emergency line with "with or without vomiting" and "right away", then the exact scoped don't-stop line. I count about 106 spoken words, inside the tight arm (90–120). There is no subscribe line and no "link in the description" line. I couldn't load the PubMed page directly because it only showed a cookie wall, but search results confirmed the record, its title and its content. Two minor wording fixes are listed for speech and muted viewing.
